title: C++ Data Structures Library
context:
Every low-latency system at a trading firm is built on hand-rolled containers: an order book is a specialised tree, a market-data buffer is a ring, a symbol map is a hash table tuned for cache lines. Before you can build those, you need to be fluent in implementing the fundamentals yourself — growth policies, amortised analysis, iterator semantics, and move semantics — without leaning on the STL.

This project produces a small C++17 library (`dsl`) of the six containers that appear in virtually every quant codebase, plus the test and benchmark scaffolding to prove they work and to measure what they cost.
problem: Implement a C++17 static library `dsl` containing `DynamicArray<T>`, `LinkedList<T>`, `HashTable<K, V>` (open addressing or chaining — your choice, documented), `BST<K, V>` (unbalanced is acceptable; document the degradation), `Heap<T, Compare>` (binary heap over a dynamic array) and `PriorityQueue<T>` (a thin, correct adapter over the heap). Provide the standard operations (insert/erase/lookup/iteration/size) with documented complexity for each, full rule-of-five semantics, no leaks, and a working CMake build with `ctest` running an assert-based unit-test suite and a microbenchmark binary reporting ns/op for representative operations.
requirements: C++17, builds with CMake >= 3.16; the build produces library target `dsl`, test executables wired into CTest, and a benchmark binary; zero warnings under `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic`.

Six containers with documented API and complexity: `DynamicArray` (amortised O(1) push_back, geometric growth), `LinkedList` (singly or doubly — document), `HashTable` (O(1) average; probing/chaining strategy documented), `BST` (O(h) operations), `Heap` (O(log n) push/pop), `PriorityQueue` (adapter over `Heap`).
Rule of five is correct everywhere: destructor, copy ctor/assign, move ctor/assign; no memory leaks (checked with ASan or valgrind in at least one run described in the README).
Containers use no STL containers internally (`std::vector` etc. are off-limits inside the implementations); raw owning pointers only inside RAII wrappers you own.
Iterator support at least for `DynamicArray` and `LinkedList` (forward iterators with begin/end, operator*, operator++, operator==); invalidation rules documented.
Unit tests per container in `tests/` using the provided assert-based harness (`DSL_TEST`/`DSL_REQUIRE`), covering empty/full/resize/erase-path cases; `ctest` runs green.
`bench/bench_containers.cpp` times push_back, lookup and erase at n = 10^4, 10^5, 10^6 and prints a table; the README explains the measured growth rates against the theory.

designGuidance.md: A dynamic array must grow geometrically or push_back degenerates to O(n) per op. Doubling gives amortised O(1) with at most ~2x memory overhead; growth factor 1.5 trades a slower growth rate for better memory reuse. Whatever you pick, write down the amortised argument: the total copy cost of n pushes with doubling is $n + (1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + n/2) < 3n$.

designGuidance.title: Why quants hand-roll containers
designGuidance.md: In market-data paths, a `std::vector<Price>` that reallocates mid-tick adds a copy spike exactly when latency matters. Production code pre-reserves or uses pooled structures. Knowing what reallocation costs — because you implemented it — is the point of this project.

rows: insert/erase O(1) at iterator, index O(n)
avg O(1), worst O(n); rehash O(n)

designGuidance.text: Move semantics are correctness, not decoration

designGuidance.caption: Move constructor and move assignment leave the source empty

designGuidance.title: Iterator invalidation is where bugs hide
designGuidance.md: Decide and document for every container: which operations invalidate which iterators/references. A `DynamicArray` realloc invalidates *everything*; a `HashTable` rehash invalidates iteration order. A test that fills a container while holding iterators and then asserts defined behaviour is worth more than ten happy-path tests.

items: Build in Release (`-O2`); never benchmark debug builds — the numbers are fiction.
Warm up each loop, run multiple repetitions, report median or best-of-k with the repetition count stated.
Use `std::chrono::steady_clock`; measure the operation, not the setup (pre-size the container outside the timed region where appropriate).
Report ns/op at n = 1e4, 1e5, 1e6 so growth behaviour (O(log n) vs O(n)) is visible in the table.

starterFiles.content:
# CMake sketch for the data-structures library.
# Expected layout (create files as you implement):
#   include/dsl/   public headers
#   src/           container implementations
#   tests/         assert-based unit tests (harness provided)
#   bench/         microbenchmarks

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(cpp_data_structures LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

if(NOT CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE)
  set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release)   # benchmarks want -O2
endif()

option(DSL_BUILD_TESTS "Build unit tests" ON)
option(DSL_BUILD_BENCHMARKS "Build microbenchmarks" ON)

enable_testing()

add_library(dsl STATIC
  src/dynamic_array.cpp
  src/linked_list.cpp
  src/hash_table.cpp
  src/bst.cpp
  src/heap.cpp
)
target_include_directories(dsl PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_compile_options(dsl PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)

if(DSL_BUILD_TESTS)
  foreach(t dynamic_array linked_list hash_table bst heap priority_queue)
    add_executable(test_${t} tests/test_${t}.cpp)
    target_link_libraries(test_${t} PRIVATE dsl)
    add_test(NAME ${t} COMMAND test_${t})
  endforeach()
endif()

if(DSL_BUILD_BENCHMARKS)
  add_executable(bench_containers bench/bench_containers.cpp)
  target_link_libraries(bench_containers PRIVATE dsl)
endif()

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctness of all six containers against their documented contracts (including edge cases)
Modern-C++ quality: RAII, rule of five, move semantics, const-correctness, no leaks
Test suite breadth: invalidation, resize, erase, copy/move independence
Benchmark methodology and match between measured growth and stated complexity
Build ergonomics (clean CMake, zero warnings) and documentation clarity

documentationRequirements: README.md: layout, build commands (`cmake -B build && cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build`), container API table with complexities, and invalidation rules per container.
Every public method carries a doc comment stating complexity and iterator/reference invalidation effects.
Benchmarks section: hardware, compiler, flags, timing table, and a paragraph comparing measured growth with theory.
extensionChallenges: Make the BST self-balancing (AVL rotations or a red-black invariant) and re-run the benchmark with sorted insert order to show the difference.
Implement a pool allocator for LinkedList/HashTable nodes and quantify the allocation-count reduction.
Add a ring buffer with head/tail indices and reuse it as the backing store for a fixed-capacity sliding window (the primitive you will need for rolling stats).
